name: Black henna (PPD)

lead: Black henna is the name given to dark pastes sold for temporary skin designs. Unlike traditional red-brown henna, which comes from the Lawsonia inermis plant, these pastes usually contain para-phenylenediamine (PPD), a hair-dye chemical, which is why they stain skin dark black quickly.

The appeal is a bold, tattoo-like look that lasts a week or two with no needle and no permanence. Dermatology literature, however, documents contact allergy to PPD after these tattoos, and sensitised people may later react to hair dye and other products.

paras: Street and holiday-resort artists apply the paste by hand or stencil and leave it on for a short time; the design darkens as the skin absorbs the dye and fades over one to two weeks. Traditional henna, by contrast, is a plant paste that stains reddish-brown over hours.

Reviews describe allergic contact dermatitis with blistering, intense itching and sometimes permanent scarring, often appearing days after application. PPD allergy can persist for life and cause reactions to hair dye and some textile dyes. Regulators such as the US FDA do not permit PPD for skin application, and dermatologists have repeatedly warned about these tattoos, especially for children.

angle.text: People choose black henna for a deep black temporary design that looks like a tattoo without permanence. The same chemistry that gives the dark colour is what dermatologists link to allergic reactions.

lead: Black henna is a term for temporary-tattoo pastes that stain skin dark black. Despite the name, such mixtures typically contain para-phenylenediamine (PPD), a chemical used in hair dye, rather than the plant dye lawsone from henna [1][2]. Red henna, the dried leaf of Lawsonia inermis, stains skin reddish-brown and is a long-standing form of body art in Islamic and Hindu cultures [2].

People use it to get a fast, dark, tattoo-like design without a permanent tattoo. The 'black henna' look took off in the 1990s when artists in tourist areas and elsewhere began applying PPD-based hair dye to skin as a thick paste [1].

The dermatology literature on black henna is large and focused on harms. Reviews report allergic contact dermatitis, sometimes severe, and cross-reactions with hair dye in people who become sensitised [2][3].

paras: Black henna is sold as a quick-staining temporary tattoo paste. The name originated in the late 19th century, when partly fermented indigo sold as 'black henna' was used with henna to darken hair, and it later came to label PPD-based skin pastes [1]. Reviews describe black henna as red henna combined with PPD [2]. Analyses of tattoo mixtures have identified PPD in them [4].

According to Wikipedia's account, PPD-based pastes began to be used on skin in the 1990s by artists in Africa, India, Bali, the Arabian Peninsula and the West who wanted fast, jet-black designs [1]. Reports of allergic reactions in holiday-makers who received such tattoos abroad appeared in the dermatology literature around 2000 [5].

A 2013 review in Contact Dermatitis found red henna generally safe, with rare contact allergy, but estimated that black henna tattoos induce contact allergy to PPD at about 2.5 percent. Sensitised people may later react to hair dyes containing PPD, with cross-reactions to some textile dyes, local anaesthetics and rubber chemicals; systemic toxicity has also been reported [2].

Case series describe people who developed severe allergic reactions to hair dye after earlier black henna tattoos [6][7]. Reactions to the tattoos themselves often appear days after application [1][5]. Dermatologists have raised particular concern about sensitisation in children [2].

In children with G6PD deficiency, a review notes that henna applied to the skin may cause life-threatening haemolysis [2]. Regulators such as the US FDA treat PPD in skin products as an adulterant [1].
Black henna is occasionally mentioned in appearance forums as a temporary-tattoo option, with discussions weighing the look against allergy risks.

Evidence consists mainly of case reports, case series and reviews rather than trials. A 2013 review pooled the literature on henna and black henna side-effects [2]. Case series from Canada and Germany document PPD hair-dye allergy following black henna tattoos [6][7]. Laboratory analysis has identified PPD in tattoo mixtures [4].

timeline.event: PPD-based pastes begin to be applied to skin as 'black henna' tattoos [1].
Archives of Dermatology reports allergic contact dermatitis after black henna skin painting [5].
CMAJ publishes six cases of hair-dye allergy after black henna tattoos [6].
Contact Dermatitis publishes a full review of henna and black henna side-effects [2].
